design_detail: Secondary-outcome report of the same uncontrolled pilot trial as Monson et al. (2020): six heterosexual couples in which one partner had PTSD, treated with a condensed 7-week course of cognitive behavioral conjoint therapy (CBCT) for PTSD with two full-day MDMA sessions for both partners, at a private practice clinic in Charleston, South Carolina. Outcomes before, at mid-treatment, after treatment and at 3 and 6 months: relationship aggression (CTS-2), post-traumatic growth (PTGI, self- and collateral-report), partner accommodation (SORTS), relationship quality (QRI), social intimacy (MSIS), psychosocial functioning (IPF) and empathy (IRI); growth-curve models and within-group effect sizes. No registration number is given in this paper; the primary report names NCT02876172. Funded through donations to MAPS. The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest, appraised with ROBINS-I.
can_establish: What happened to self- and partner-reported relationship, growth, functioning and empathy measures over 6 months in six couples given CBCT with two MDMA sessions, and that minor psychological aggression did not rise in this small group with low baseline aggression.
cannot_establish: Whether any change is due to MDMA, to CBCT or to time and expectation (no comparison group); whether the intervention is safe for couples with relationship aggression (severe aggression was excluded and baseline aggression was low); or anything about couples other than White, mixed-gender couples.

sample.recruitment: Not described here; the paper refers to Monson et al. (2020) for the full study description (Method › Participants, 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Both partners 18 or older, with no current substance use disorder, no active suicidal planning or intent, no mania, psychosis or severe partner aggression (severe aggression on the CTS-2 sexual coercion or physical aggression subscales was exclusionary); all psychiatric medicines tapered off; medical screening for essential hypertension, cardiac disorder and other major medical conditions (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Measures › Relationship Aggression Outcomes).
sample.demographics: Average age about 47; all White; all mixed-gender couples; patients: two women, all with comorbid diagnoses and earlier psychological and drug treatment for PTSD, five of six with multiple traumas; partners: four women, 50% with psychological diagnoses (Method › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: No dropout is reported; the paper says every outcome had at most one or two missing data points (at most 30%) at any assessment (Data Analyses, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: As in Monson et al. (2020): self-selected couples willing to take MDMA together, treated by the developers of the therapy; relationship depth was already high at baseline, which the authors attribute to self-selection (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, given to all: CBCT for PTSD over 7 weeks (five modules in 1.5 days before MDMA session one, six between the two MDMA sessions, four weekly after the second) with two full-day MDMA sessions in reclining chairs with eyeshades, headphones and music, alternating inward focus with conversation with the therapists and partner; MDMA sessions placed after the communication-skills work and in the middle of trauma processing (Method › Procedure, 1st to 4th paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: 75 mg MDMA in the first session with an optional supplemental 37.5 mg 1.5 hours later; 100 mg in the second session with an optional 50 mg at 1.5 hours; both partners dosed (Method › Procedure, 4th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Current substance use disorder excluded (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph); drug use during the study not reported.

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as such; CBCT itself, time, regression to the mean and expectation are uncontrolled.

outcomes.instruments: CTS-2 (39 tactics, used and experienced; negotiation, psychological aggression, physical assault, sexual coercion, injury); PTGI (21 items; completed by both partners about the patient, the partner version edited into a collateral report for this study); SORTS (14 items, partner only, frequency and intensity of accommodation, 0 to 4); QRI (25 items; support, conflict, depth); IPF (80 items; higher scores mean more impairment); MSIS (17 items); IRI (28 items; perspective taking, fantasy, empathic concern, personal distress) (Measures, all subsections).
outcomes.validity_norms: Published internal consistencies are cited for each measure; the collateral-report version of the PTGI is new to this study and has no validation reported (Measures › Trauma-Related Outcomes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Change over time in growth-curve models (log-transformed days since baseline; fixed slopes and random intercepts, kept for parsimony because the better-fitting random-slope model did not converge in most cases); within-group Cohen's d from pre-treatment to each time point on estimated means and raw pooled SDs (Data Analyses, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Editors' count of the models reported: six CTS-2 models (patients' minor psychological aggression, minor physical assault, emotional and cognitive negotiation; partners' emotional and cognitive negotiation), PTGI 2, SORTS 1, QRI 6, MSIS 2, IPF 2, IRI 8.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: all measures are self- or partner-reports by people who had taken MDMA.

analysis.effect_sizes: Growth-model slopes (B, SE) and within-group d ranges (mid-treatment to 6 months): PTGI rated by patients B = 7.30 (1.56), d 1.44 to 2.00, and by partners B = 7.63 (1.49), d 1.76 to 2.74, both P < 0.001; SORTS (partners) B = −3.86 (1.36), P < 0.01, d 1.01 to 1.78; QRI support, patients B = 0.06 (0.03), P = 0.041, partners B = 0.08 (0.03), P = 0.029; QRI conflict, patients P = 0.062, partners B = −0.09 (0.03), P = 0.002; QRI depth not significant; MSIS intimacy, patients B = 4.12 (1.32), P = 0.005, d 0.93 to 1.31, partners B = 3.10 (1.03), P = 0.007, d 0.41 to 0.68; IPF, patients B = −3.20 (0.69), P < 0.001, d 0.95 to 1.26, partners P = 0.299; IRI empathic concern, patients B = 0.69 (0.32), P = 0.037, d 0.58 to 0.95, partners and other subscales not significant; CTS-2, patients' minor psychological aggression B = −0.98 (0.21), P < 0.001, d 1.06 to 1.56, no change in minor physical assault, other aggression models not estimable (Results, all subsections; Tables 1 and 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: This paper gives no registration; the primary report names ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172, whose registered secondary outcomes (read for the Monson et al. card) do not include the CTS-2, PTGI, SORTS, QRI, IPF, MSIS or IRI.
analysis.selective_reporting: These relational measures are not registered outcomes of the trial; models for several CTS-2 scales could not be estimated because of infrequent endorsement.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In six couples who completed CBCT with two MDMA sessions, patients' post-traumatic growth (rated by both partners), partners' accommodation, perceived support, social intimacy, patients' psychosocial functioning and empathic concern improved between baseline and 6 months; relationship depth, most empathy subscales and partners' functioning did not change; minor psychological aggression fell in patients. None of these changes can be attributed to MDMA, and the printed SORTS means are a copy of another measure (reporting issues).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the findings suggest that CBCT with MDMA "has significant effect on relational and growth outcomes" in this pilot sample (Abstract). The Discussion says the results demonstrate that the combination provides improvements for both partners and the relationship and that the intervention is safe and does not increase the risk of relational or interpersonal harm (Discussion, 1st paragraph), and that a feeling of connection during MDMA sessions likely played a role in improved intimacy, though not formally tested (Discussion, 4th paragraph). The Limitations acknowledge that, by design, no conclusion about efficacy relative to placebo or to either component alone can be drawn (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

timeline.event: Monson et al., Eur J Psychotraumatol: primary outcomes of the same six couples (not independent of this paper).
This paper: relational and growth outcomes.

replication.where_it_stands: Same sample as Monson et al. (2020); no independent or controlled study of these relational outcomes is among the sources read.

funding.funder: Donations to MAPS; a MAPS-sponsored study, and the funder had input into the study design (Footnotes › Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: CM receives royalties from Guilford Press for the CBCT manual; AW, MM, AM and CM received salary support from MAPS for the study; MM and AM sit on the advisory board of Awakn Life Sciences; the remaining author declares no conflicts (Conflict of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The authors designed and ran the study (Author Contributions); the first and last authors are among the therapy's developers. Raw data available from the authors (Data Availability Statement).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison of CBCT with MDMA against CBCT with an active placebo, with registered relational outcomes, observer-rated couple interaction, measured expectancy and a follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: No comparison group; the intervention includes a full course of CBCT, so no change can be attributed to MDMA.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Self-selected couples, already high in relationship depth; severe aggression excluded.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Co-interventions are not reported here (the primary report shows three of six patients in current psychotherapy at baseline).
Up to one or two of six values missing per assessment for some outcomes; which ones is not reported.
Self- and partner-reports by people who took MDMA, about a therapy delivered by its developers; one measure (collateral PTGI) was adapted for this study without validation.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: None of these outcomes is registered; 27 models without correction; the SORTS means printed in Table 1 are not the SORTS data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: An uncontrolled secondary analysis of six couples: as evidence that MDMA improves relationships it is at critical risk of bias. It can be cited for the observed course of these self-reports and for the absence of an increase in minor aggression in this small, low-aggression sample; it cannot be cited for effects of MDMA, for safety in couples with aggression, or for the SORTS values in Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Same six couples as the primary report; patients two women and four men, partners four women and two men; all White and mixed-gender; treated at a private practice clinic in Charleston, South Carolina.

Post-traumatic growth of the patient: rated by patients 19.40 (SD 10.29) before treatment, 64.17 (32.43) after and 63.50 (27.36) at 6 months, B = 7.30 (SE 1.56), d 1.44 to 2.00; rated by partners 14.60 (15.77), 55.75 (16.46) and 55.67 (15.32), B = 7.63 (1.49), d 1.76 to 2.74; both P < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes › Trauma-Related Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Partner accommodation (SORTS): B = −3.86 (SE 1.36), P < 0.01, d 1.01 to 1.78; the means printed for SORTS in Table 1 (49.58 [8.52] before treatment to 16.64 [14.84] at 6 months) are identical, value for value, to the partner-rated PCL-5 means in the primary report's Table 2.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes › Trauma-Related Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (SORTS row); Table 2
key_findings.note: The modelled result (B, d) may be right, but the printed SORTS means cannot be cited (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Relationship quality (QRI): support improved for patients (B = 0.06, P = 0.041; d 0.68 to 0.94) and partners (B = 0.08, P = 0.029; d 0.47 to 0.81); conflict fell for partners (B = −0.09, P = 0.002) but not significantly for patients (P = 0.062); depth did not change (patients P = 0.171, partners P = 0.093).
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes › Relationship Quality Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2
Results › Outcomes › Relationship Quality Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Tables 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Psychosocial functioning (IPF, higher = more impairment): patients 52.35 (14.48) to 35.94 after treatment and 34.14 at 6 months, B = −3.20 (0.69), P < 0.001, d 0.95 to 1.26; partners no significant change (B = −0.67, P = 0.299). Empathy (IRI): patients' empathic concern rose (B = 0.69, P = 0.037, d 0.58 to 0.95); no change in partners' empathic concern or in personal distress, fantasy or perspective taking for either partner.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes › Psychosocial Functioning Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Relationship aggression (CTS-2): patients' minor psychological aggression fell (B = −0.98, SE 0.21, P < 0.001, d 1.06 to 1.56); no significant change in patients' minor physical assault; the other aggression models could not be estimated because these items were rarely endorsed; negotiation strategies did not change.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety Outcomes › Relationship Aggression, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The SORTS (partner) row of Table 1 reproduces exactly the partner-rated PCL-5 estimated means and SDs of the primary report (Monson et al., 2020, Table 2): 49.58 (8.52), 26.38 (19.37), 21.54 (19.67), 19.08 (16.18), 16.64 (14.84). The SORTS growth estimate (B = −3.86) and effect sizes (1.01 to 1.78) differ from the PCL-5 ones (B = −5.90; 1.55 to 2.72).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1; Results › Outcomes › Trauma-Related Outcomes, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed SORTS means are a copying error and cannot be cited; whether the modelled SORTS results were computed on the right data cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 is titled 'Estimated means and standard deviations', but its footnote says raw means and standard deviations are presented, while Table 2's footnote says the effect sizes were computed from least-squares means estimated from growth models.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1 title and footnote; Table 2 footnote)
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether Table 1 holds observed or estimated values; recomputing the effect sizes from it may not reproduce Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: Missing data are described as at most 1 to 2 data points, 'maximum 30%', per assessment; 2 of 6 is 33%. Several Table 1 means (for example PTGI 19.40 and 14.60 before treatment) can only come from five people.
reporting_issues.consequence: Some time points rest on five of six participants.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper calls the treatment safe and says it does not increase the risk of relational or interpersonal harm, but severe aggression was an exclusion criterion, baseline aggression was low, and most partner aggression models could not be estimated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 1st paragraph; Measures › Relationship Aggression Outcomes; Results › Safety Outcomes)
reporting_issues.consequence: The safety statement concerns six low-aggression couples only.

reporting_issues.issue: The background cites the pooled phase 2 analysis (Mithoefer et al., 2019; reference 22), which PMC's reference list marks as retracted, for the promising results of individual MDMA-assisted therapy.
reporting_issues.consequence: Background only; not used by the card.
